page: Google Cloud Platform n1-standard-96 is a general-purpose virtual machine belonging to the N1 server family. It features 96 vCPUs mapped to 48 physical cores of an Intel Xeon processor using x86_64 architecture. The system is configured with 360 GB of dedicated RAM, providing 3.75 GB of memory per core. It does not include bundled local storage or GPUs, and has no complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Performance benchmarks indicate a clear trade-off between single-core and multi-core capabilities. Single-core performance is relatively weak, scoring in the bottom 25% for stress-ng, Geekbench, and single-threaded compression tasks. However, multi-core CPU performance is strong, placing in the top 25% on stress-ng. Memory bandwidth is also a notable strength, with both read and write operations on large uncached blocks scoring in the top 25%.

Given its hardware profile, the n1-standard-96 offers a balanced resource density suitable for highly parallelized workloads that can leverage its 96 vCPUs and strong memory bandwidth, such as multi-threaded compilation, database operations, and static web serving. However, it is less efficient for single-threaded tasks or real-time LLM text generation, where it exhibits weak to poor performance. From a cost-efficiency perspective, it provides a high density of legacy Intel Xeon cores and memory, making it a viable option for legacy enterprise applications and parallel batch processing that do not require modern instruction sets like AMX or AVX-512 VNNI.
description: Google Cloud Platform n1-standard-96 is an x86_64 general-purpose server powered by an Intel Xeon processor with 96 vCPUs (48 physical cores) and 360 GB of dedicated RAM. It does not feature local storage or GPU accelerators. Benchmarks reveal a significant performance divergence: single-core execution and single-threaded compression are weak, falling into the bottom 25%, whereas multi-core CPU performance and memory bandwidth are strong, ranking in the top 25%. The instance supports AVX and AVX-512F instructions but lacks newer extensions like AMX. It is qualitatively cost-effective for highly parallelized workloads, such as multi-threaded software compilation, database operations, and static web serving, which benefit from its high core count and high memory bandwidth, rather than single-threaded or modern AI inference tasks.
